What really does shine is Rickson's mastery of Chekhov’s humour, in a production that never feels drawn-out or stodgy.

Rickson’s direction is masterful, alive to every nuance, confidently embracing the dualities in Chekhov’s text: these people are deeply unhappy yet uproariously funny, and the sense of lives about to change forever is keenly felt.
The message about those who fail to move with the times being left behind rings loud and clear in this insightful and surprisingly sprightly production.

Scott Thomas gives a beautifully subtle, modulated performance as Ranevskaya, conveying both her privileged detachment from day-to-day concerns, and ongoing grief for her son that leads her to seek consolation abroad and neglect her much-loved home.
A compelling production, and worth the watch for Kristin Scott Thomas’s performance alone, this new adaptation proves the enduring relevance of The Cherry Orchard.

This new adaptation by Conor McPherson has arrived at the Harold Pinter Theatre with a stellar cast, Stephen Mangan as Lopakhin, Kristen Scott Thomas as Lyubov Andreevna (Luba) and Ruby Bentall as Sharlotta.
All in all, this is a fun and touching restaging of a classic family drama...
McPherson’s adaptation is expletive-laden and very frank, highlighting the hypocrisy of a family who cannot articulate their feelings or act in a way that serves their interest.
For all its thoughtful performances and its strong depiction of a family, and a society, in transition, the play struggles to feel really enduring and universal.
As such, Rickson and McPherson’s The Cherry Orchard is far more entertaining than it is intellectual and emotive, meaning it ought to have been a lot more fruitful.

cn.t: Critics praise Kristin Scott Thomas's luminous performance and Ian Rickson's atmospheric direction in this Chekhov revival, though responses to Conor McPherson's contemporary adaptation divide—some find it accessible and witty, others feel it lacks depth and emotional resonance.

vr.q: This production of The Cherry Orchard is a masterful reimagining from Conor McPherson that is brought to life by perfect cast and Ian Rickson's impeccable direction.
For me, I don't think that it particularly worked, and that's because it undermines what is to follow.
